To peeve someone means to mildly irritate, annoy, or bother them — to get under their skin in a low-level, nagging way.

It's not a strong, explosive word. When someone is peeved, they're not furious or outraged. They're experiencing that specific, slightly simmering feeling you get when something keeps bothering you — like a stone in your shoe that you can't shake out.

Think of the feeling when someone repeatedly clicks their pen in a quiet room, when a colleague takes credit for your idea in a meeting, or when your roommate never replaces the toilet paper roll. That quiet, gnawing irritation — that's what being peeved feels like.

"Peeve" as a verb is transitive, meaning it always acts on someone. Something or someone peeves you — the irritation lands on a person.

The most common patterns are:

  • Something peeves someone:
    • "His constant lateness peeves her."
    • "That loud chewing really peeves me."
  • Someone is peeved at/about/by something:
    • "She was peeved at him for forgetting."
    • "He's peeved about being left out."
    • "I was peeved by her remark."

Notice that "peeved" — the past tense / past participle — is extremely common and is often used as an adjective to describe a person's emotional state:

  • "She gave him a peeved look."
  • "He walked away looking peeved."
  • "Why do you seem peeved?"

This is important, because English has many words for annoyance and getting this right will make you sound natural.

"Peeve" sits on the mild-to-moderate end of the irritation scale. Here's a rough sense of the range:

Peeved → Annoyed → Irritated → Frustrated → Angry → Furious

Being peeved is toward the left — it's a quiet, low-burning feeling. You might roll your eyes, give a cold stare, or sigh heavily when you're peeved. You wouldn't scream or slam doors. It often has a slightly sulky or wounded quality to it — like you feel a small injustice has been done to you.

Register: When Do People Use This Word?

"Peeve" is an informal, everyday word. You'd use it in casual conversation, in personal writing, in social media posts, or in light, informal articles. You wouldn't use it in a formal report or a legal document.

It's also a very relatable, human word — when someone says "that peeves me," it usually lands with a bit of self-awareness or even mild humor, acknowledging that the annoyance is perhaps a small thing but genuinely bothersome.
The Noun Form: "A Peeve" and "A Pet Peeve"

Knowing the noun is essential to fully understanding the word's world.

  • A peeve = a specific thing that annoys you.
    • "One of my peeves is people who talk during movies."
  • A pet peeve = a particular thing that especially and repeatedly bothers you — something you personally find very irritating, even if others don't.
    • "My biggest pet peeve is bad grammar."
    • "Slow walkers in busy corridors are a real pet peeve of mine."

"Pet peeve" is a very widely used phrase in everyday English.
To peeve is to mildly but genuinely irritate someone — not enough to make them rage, but enough to leave them silently bothered, slightly sulky, and very aware of the annoyance.
